item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Bug: README.md doesn't disappear from ls after you rm it. 592-scan-01.jpg doesn't exist but mind-melts you anyway. (It presumably isn't actually a scan of 592, as those are never saved to nonvolatile memory per the SCPs)

Not a bug, but an oversight that might well be Dr Ashley's: The man page for cleansum doesn't give any 'out of' information, making it really easy to melt your brain if you assume it's out of 10 or 100 :P

I have to agree that the payoff really isn't worth it. Especially when it's kind of illogical, wouldn't gnupg look in .gnupg by default? How did anyone but Dr. Ashley have Dr. Ashley's password anyway? It would have made more sense to log in as Kendal and use sudo to bypass the permissions issues. Is the Foundation really not using one of the several ways to have logins synced across many machines?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I like the solution to the problem I had in SCP-2111 and am considering implementing this there, and the puzzle was fun (although I am a little perplexed about why deleting README.txt makes the memscan utility suddenly available) but I ultimately downvoted for the ending that is so anticlimactic and meaningless that it feels like it must be deliberately so. I didn't no-vote, because anything would have been a better payoff than a blank document, so this seems to be a deliberate exercise is reader frustration, and because the author wastefully discarded the natural opportunity to advance the plot of the series.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I was torn between a neutral and an up-vote. As a part of the MTF contest, I presume it's purpose is to get you to think from the point of view of a rho-9 flunky, and it works for that. And the puzzle gimmick was clever, despite being gimmicky. And I liked the puzzle. And the images (er, "like" isn't really the right word for that first one, since I think it was a real-life cognito-hazard, but you know what I mean.)

However, I felt it relied to heavily on the gimmick, and failed to deliver enough of a payoff. You finally solve the puzzle and are rewarded with… a(n apparently) blank document? You don't discover any narrative or information at all?

I upvoted before I finished solving the puzzle (before I knew there was no payoff). I've switched it to a neutral this morning, (sorry). This format could have allowed for some interesting (possibly fragmented) storytelling. But the only real interest came from the puzzle itself.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I had initially upvoted this, and I really like this kind of adventure article, but it feels like it's incomplete or rushed. The attention to detail (the man pages are <3) is keeping me from downvoting it. Feels like you put time into this, but then ran out of time on the contest deadline and needed to get it out.

I think this has potential if more content or recovered data was added past the ending, or at least a little more closure than "please go to security because memetic hazard," or the circumstances behind the good Doc Ashley's disappearance.

Canceling my vote.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Is this super gimmicky? Y [x] N [ ]

Is this original? Y[ ] N[x]

Am I able to enjoy this story while drunk? Y[ ] N[x]

Is there enough to make me care about trying to try to click my way through a bunch of false starts when there are better ways to spend my time? Y[ ] N[x]

Even after I do sort my way through it, do I find anything interesting? Y[ ] N[X]

EDIT: Okay, I might as well elaborate a bit. this is what happened when Silber took a shot at a similar concept. Take a look at it. Even the false starts are cleverly done. The story gives you a good reward/effort return (as opposed to this, which gives low satisfaction for high effort), and is actually interesting. Even the throwaway parts that are just meant to get you to click back give you something unique and cool to read. Because that's how stories should be. Everything should have a purpose, everything should give the reader some reason to care about reading further. This actively works against me giving a shit.

So basically I'm saying that this is a small amount of content buried under a hill of nothing, using a cheap trick that isn't particularly groundbreaking or unique to try to hide that fact.

A brief summary of my standards.
